(The FOX Sports odds page lists a shorter FOX Bet price of -556, ~84.7% implied.) As an independent model cross-check, the Opta supercomputer's Monte-Carlo simulation priced the match Argentina 80.2% / Draw 12.9% / Saudi Arabia 6.9% pre-match. Both real systems agreed Argentina was a heavy favourite; the result (Saudi 6.9% per Opta) was one of the most improbable in World Cup history and a near-worst-case Brier outcome for any favourite-backing forecaster.

narrative.storyline: Renard's high line weaponised — Argentina drowned in offsides
narrative.text: Hervé Renard kept Saudi Arabia's back four pushed aggressively high all match, daring Argentina to run in behind. It backfired on Argentina: per Opta, Argentina were flagged offside six times inside the first 32 minutes — more than any team managed in a full match at the entire 2018 World Cup — and seven times before half-time. The trap turned Argentina's pace and through-ball game into a self-defeating weapon and choked the midfield space Messi works in.
narrative.why: The single tactical mechanism that decided the game: it neutralised Argentina's chance-creation edge and chalked off goals, letting a 0.14-xG Saudi side stay level long enough to win.

narrative.storyline: Three Argentina goals chalked off — Lautaro twice, margins of millimetres
narrative.text: Argentina had the ball in the net three more times and saw all three ruled out for offside via semi-automated technology — two of them Lautaro Martínez goals decided by an armpit/shoulder being marginal inches beyond the last defender. Fans and analysts argued at least one (with left-back Yasser Al-Shahrani appearing to play Lautaro on) was harshly called. Had any stood, the upset likely never happens.
narrative.why: The fine-margin turning point: the scoreline that looked like comfortable Argentine control was actually held to 1-0 by millimetric VAR lines, leaving the door open.

narrative.storyline: Renard's halftime masterstroke and Saudi grit after going 1-0 down
narrative.text: Despite an early Messi penalty and relentless first-half pressure, Renard did not retreat — he doubled down on the high press at the break, crushing the space between Saudi lines and refusing to sit deep. Saudi Arabia, who had zero shots in the first half, came out and struck twice in five minutes, riding a wave of belief and physical commitment (they out-fouled Argentina 21 to 7) to hold the line for 37+ minutes after taking the lead.
narrative.why: The human/motivation story behind the comeback: a coach's nerve and a squad's collective resolve converting a hopeless xG profile into a famous win.

narrative.storyline: Messi's last-dance opener and the end of a 36-game unbeaten run
narrative.text: Messi converted a 10th-minute penalty (won via VAR for Saud Abdulhamid's shirt-pull on Paredes) to become the fifth player to score at four different World Cups — a dream start to his final World Cup. By full time it was a nightmare: Argentina's 36-match unbeaten run was over, drawing comparisons to Cameroon shocking Maradona's Argentina in 1990, and casting immediate doubt over the eventual champions' campaign.
narrative.why: The human arc and stakes — the tournament's defining what-the-hell moment for the eventual winners, and the personal weight on Messi's last World Cup.

magic_moment.text: Al-Dawsari took the ball out of the air on the edge of the box, danced past both Nahuel Molina and Ángel Di María, and curled a right-footed shot high into the far top corner past Emiliano Martínez — a goal of the tournament contender that completed the comeback. Sky's call: 'Time stood still as Al-Dawsari plucked the ball out from the sky and turned inside two Argentina defenders before curling his finish beyond the reach of Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.' Saudi fans chanted 'Our team fulfils our dreams!'
magic_moment.why: The decisive winner and the image of the upset — a 0.05-xG strike (per soccer-blogger) of breathtaking individual quality that beat one of the world's best keepers and the eventual world champions.

magic_moment.text: Three minutes into the second half, Al-Shehri pounced on hesitancy from Cristian Romero, cut inside and flashed a low right-footed shot across Martínez into the bottom corner to level at 1-1 — Saudi Arabia's first shot on target of the match and the goal that flipped the script.
magic_moment.why: The equaliser that broke the dam: Saudi's first real chance, taken clinically, igniting the five-minute window that won the game.

stats.text: Argentina generated ~2.16 xG (xgscore.io) to ~2.29 (soccer-blogger) — a dominant chance profile, yet they lost. Models differ by provider; both put Argentina well above 2.0 xG.
Saudi Arabia won on just 0.14 xG per Opta — the lowest xG a team has needed to win a World Cup match since 1966. xgscore.io's model has it at 0.35. Either way, the lowest-quality-chances side won.

narrative.storyline: Mexico's defensive 5-3-2 stifled Argentina until it backfired
narrative.text: Tata Martino abandoned his usual 4-3-3 for a defensive 5-3-2, packing numbers in central areas. It initially frustrated La Albiceleste, but in the second half Argentina exploited the shape on the flanks — Jesús Gallardo 'looked overwhelmed when Argentina roamed onto his area' — and the structure that had kept the first half scoreless ultimately cracked.
narrative.why: The match was decided as much by Mexico's containment plan collapsing in the second half as by Argentine quality; the tactical tweak that worked for 64 minutes failed at the decisive moment.

narrative.storyline: A must-win after the Saudi shock — 'another World Cup starts'
narrative.text: The opening defeat to Saudi Arabia meant defeat here would have all but eliminated Argentina after two games, ending Messi's final World Cup bid. Messi framed the stakes himself: 'After the goal, we became again who we are... we needed this result, we needed this euphoria in this game that we had to win.'
narrative.why: Motivation and pressure were the central human story: this was effectively a knockout game disguised as a group fixture, and the psychological release after Messi's goal reset the entire tournament for Argentina.

narrative.storyline: An attritional, record-low-quality contest broken by one moment
narrative.text: The first half was the lowest-quality of the entire tournament to that point — barely any clear chances, with Opta logging just ~0.28 combined xG across the opening 45 (the lowest combined first-half xG of the 2022 World Cup). Argentina dominated the ball (67.3% first-half possession) but their 'boring possession' recalled the laboured 2018 midfield until Messi's strike unlocked it.
narrative.why: Frames why the favourite needed individual brilliance rather than sustained chance creation: the game state was a low-event stalemate where one piece of magic, not territorial dominance, was always likely to be the difference.

narrative.storyline: Enzo Fernández announces himself; Messi turns provider
narrative.text: Substitute Enzo Fernández (on from the 57th minute) sealed it in the 87th, cutting inside from the left after a Messi-worked corner and curling 'a sumptuous finish' past Guillermo Ochoa — with Messi supplying the assist. At 21 years, 10 months and 13 days, he became the second-youngest player ever to score a World Cup goal for Argentina, behind only Messi.
narrative.why: The killer second goal marked the emergence of a future Argentina midfield star and showed Messi shifting from scorer to creator — a generational handover moment inside the result.

magic_moment.text: With the game deadlocked, Di María rolled it to Messi ~25 yards out and Messi rifled a low, precise strike into the bottom corner past Ochoa — his 93rd Argentina goal and 8th at World Cups, equalling Diego Maradona's tally. The Lusail crowd erupted; it was the single moment that revived Argentina's whole campaign.
magic_moment.why: This is the node's decisive moment: a near-elimination must-win, broken by a vintage Messi long-ranger that swung Argentina's tournament from the brink back to favourites.

magic_moment.text: Three minutes from time, substitute Enzo Fernández cut inside from the left off a Messi-assisted corner and curled a sumptuous finish into the far top corner past Ochoa — a goal pundits said 'rivalled Messi's' — to make it 2-0 and secure the result beyond doubt.
magic_moment.why: The insurance goal that confirmed the win and depended only on Argentina themselves; a star-is-born moment for the 21-year-old.

stats.text: Per-side full-match xG: Argentina 0.53, Mexico 0.37. Both sides drastically over-performed their chance quality — Argentina scored twice from just 0.53 xG, underlining that the result hinged on finishing quality (Messi's long-ranger) rather than chance volume.

narrative.storyline: Scaloni's positional fluidity overwhelmed a passive Poland block
narrative.text: Argentina lined up in a fluid 4-4-2 with Messi roaming centrally and Álvarez replacing Lautaro Martínez for extra mobility, while Poland sat in a deep, compact 4-4-1-1 designed purely to limit Argentina's chances. Scaloni's licence for his players to drift off their nominal positions pulled Poland's lines apart; Argentina recorded their highest-ever World Cup passing volume (800 passes, 92% completion, since 1966), suffocating Poland into 27% possession and zero shots on target.
narrative.why: This is the tactical 'why' behind the scoreline — not luck but a deliberate fluid-possession structure dismantling a low block.

narrative.storyline: Messi's best tournament display so far — the penalty miss didn't break him
narrative.text: Messi produced his standout performance of Qatar 2022 — 98 touches, five dribbles, five chances created, involved in almost every attack — even though Szczęsny brilliantly saved his VAR-awarded first-half penalty. The human storyline was Argentina's composure: rather than letting the miss derail them, they came out and scored within a minute of the restart. Mac Allister said the side resolved to 'stay positive, to stay calm' after the spot-kick.
narrative.why: Distinct from tactics — the key-player and psychology arc that defined the match's mood and Messi's redemption framing.

narrative.storyline: Poland survived by goal difference while being thoroughly outplayed — the cynical-survival subplot
narrative.text: Poland advanced in second place purely on goal difference over Mexico, and coach Czesław Michniewicz openly instructed his players to 'avoid silly bookings' to protect a fair-play / goal-difference tiebreak as news of Saudi Arabia v Mexico filtered through. Lewandowski did not register a single shot. The narrative wasn't Poland's resistance but their pragmatic, almost passive, qualification by the back door.
narrative.why: The losing side's motivation story — qualifying by tiebreak math, not performance — a separate human/strategic thread from Argentina's dominance.

magic_moment.text: 46' — Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring within a minute of the restart, meeting Nahuel Molina's low cut-back from the right with a first-time, slightly scuffed finish that trickled past Szczęsny and in off the far post. The timing was the broadcast story: it instantly washed away the first-half frustration of the missed Messi penalty and released the dam Argentina had been building.
magic_moment.why: The decisive opener — it converted total territorial dominance into a lead at the psychologically perfect moment, right after the penalty miss.

magic_moment.text: 67' — Julián Álvarez collected an Enzo Fernández pass and curled a brilliant left-footed finish past Szczęsny to make it 2-0, killing the contest and confirming Argentina would top Group C.
magic_moment.why: The killer second goal — sealed the group win and underlined Álvarez's emergence as the mobile striker Scaloni's system needed.

narrative.storyline: Argentina's build-up overload broke Australia's mid-block
narrative.text: Breaking The Lines' tactical analysis shows Argentina dropping Messi and Rodrigo De Paul into central zones to create a 3-v-2 advantage against Australia's 4-4-2 mid-block, pinning the Socceroos' midfielders and freeing the full-backs to progress. Argentina's clearest tactical superiority came in this second-phase build-up — they out-numbered Australia's first pressing line and walked the ball into the final third.
narrative.why: Explains why Argentina dominated possession (61%) without ever being seriously pressed in the first hour.

narrative.storyline: Messi's 1000th game and first-ever World Cup knockout goal
narrative.text: ESPN framed the night around Messi's 1,000th career match: the curling left-footed 35th-minute opener was his first knockout-stage goal in five World Cups. Australia boss Graham Arnold told ESPN 'He is incredible. One of the greatest ever,' likening facing him to facing Maradona — the human story that carried the broadcast.
narrative.why: The dominant pre/post-match storyline; a milestone moment that decided the game's emotional and competitive arc.

narrative.storyline: Australia's high-press gamble backfired into the second goal
narrative.text: Per Breaking The Lines, Australia's intense high press left defensive vulnerabilities; after going behind they shifted to an even more aggressive 'Plan B' that surrendered their backline numerical balance. ESPN's report ties this to the killer second goal: keeper Mat Ryan's slack touch under pressure let Julián Álvarez rob him and finish into an open net just after half-time, punishing exactly the risk Australia took.
narrative.why: The turning point — Australia's tactical trade-off directly produced the 2-0 error that put the tie effectively out of reach.

narrative.storyline: The late Socceroos scare — a deflected goal and a stoppage-time chance
narrative.text: ESPN documented Australia's late rally: Craig Goodwin's 77th-minute strike from outside the box deflected in (off Enzo Fernández) to make it 2-1, then Aziz Behich beat four defenders before Lisandro Martínez's recovery tackle, and substitute Garang Kuol forced a stoppage-time save from Emiliano Martínez. Argentina were rattled but held on.
narrative.why: The closing tension — why a 'routine' favourite hold became a genuine scare, and the human drama of Australia nearly forcing extra time.

magic_moment.text: Messi's 35th-minute opener: starting a move from the right, a one-two carried him into the box and he curled a low left-footed finish past Mat Ryan — his first goal in a World Cup knockout tie, on his 1,000th career appearance. FOX's broadcast built its narrative around the legend finally breaking through at the business end of a World Cup.
magic_moment.why: The decisive, era-defining goal: Messi's first WC knockout strike on his 1,000th game broke a tense deadlock and set Argentina on the path that ended with the title.

magic_moment.text: Álvarez's 57th-minute goal: pressing keeper Mat Ryan as he tried to play out, Álvarez dispossessed him and rolled into an empty net for 2-0 — a clean piece of front-foot pressure that, on broadcast, looked like the goal that ended the tie.
magic_moment.why: The second goal that should have killed the game; punished Australia's keeper error and Argentina's pressing trap.

magic_moment.text: Goodwin's 77th-minute strike from outside the box deflected in (officially credited to Goodwin; the deflection came off Enzo Fernández) to make it 2-1 and reignite the tie, feeding the late drama that nearly produced a Kuol equaliser in stoppage time.
magic_moment.why: Turned a comfortable lead into a nervy finish — the moment that made the match a genuine knockout scare rather than a procession.

narrative.storyline: Scaloni's tactical switch to a back-three smothered the Dutch threat for 80 minutes
narrative.text: Lionel Scaloni shifted Argentina to a 3-5-2, adding a third centre-back (Lisandro Martínez alongside Romero and Otamendi) with Molina and Acuña as wing-backs. The extra defender plus a three-man midfield (Enzo Fernández, De Paul, Mac Allister) choked the wings and half-spaces where the Netherlands wanted to hurt them, leaving Memphis Depay and Bergwijn starved of service. The Dutch managed barely a single meaningful shot before the 80th minute — Argentina's block, not Messi's flashes, was the platform for a 2–0 lead.
narrative.why: Explains WHY Argentina dominated to 2–0: a structural plan that neutralised Dutch wing/counter threats, not luck.

narrative.storyline: Van Gaal's pre-match jabs at Messi became Argentina's fuel — and the post-match flashpoint
narrative.system: Wikipedia 'Battle of Lusail' (event record, citing Van Gaal/Messi quotes)
narrative.text: Louis van Gaal had said Messi 'does not play much when he has possession… that is where our chances lie.' After his penalty Messi cupped his ears toward the Dutch bench in a pointed celebration, and post-match aimed '¿Qué mirás, bobo?' ('What are you looking at, fool?') at Wout Weghorst. The needle ran through the whole night and defined its character as much as the football.
narrative.why: Distinct HUMAN storyline (motivation/feud), separate from tactics and odds; it is what the match is culturally remembered for.

narrative.storyline: The 'Battle of Lusail': referee Mateu Lahoz lost control of the most ill-tempered match of the tournament
narrative.text: The tie grew increasingly contentious, tensions spilling between players and benches. Referee Antonio Mateu Lahoz brandished a World Cup-record 18 yellow cards (plus a late red to Denzel Dumfries), drawing widespread criticism for losing control. The Netherlands committed 30 fouls to Argentina's 18 — a chaos that ironically helped fuel the late Dutch surge.
narrative.why: A turning-point/atmosphere storyline: the descent into chaos created the conditions for the 80th-minute Dutch revival.

narrative.storyline: Emi Martínez's shootout heroics and mind-games settled a tie Argentina had nearly thrown away
narrative.system: Opta Analyst / The Analyst (preview & shootout context)
narrative.text: After surrendering a two-goal lead in the last ten minutes, Argentina were dragged to penalties for the second straight World Cup meeting with the Dutch. Emiliano Martínez — Argentina's most reliable shot-stopper of the tournament — saved from Virgil van Dijk and Steven Berghuis, his gamesmanship rattling the Dutch takers, before Lautaro Martínez buried the decider for a 4–3 win.
narrative.why: Key-player storyline at the decisive phase: the keeper, not the attack, won the tie — a different actor from the goalscoring narrative.

magic_moment.text: Weghorst's 90+11' equaliser — the rehearsed free-kick that broke Argentine hearts. Deep into an extraordinary 11 minutes of stoppage time, the Netherlands ran a worked routine: instead of crossing, Teun Koopmeiners rolled the dead ball square under the wall to substitute Wout Weghorst, who swept it in to make it 2–2 and force extra time. Weghorst's two goals carried a combined xG of just ~0.20 — a barely-believable rescue from a tactical set-piece, and the moment that turned a routine Argentina win into the 'Battle of Lusail'.
magic_moment.why: The single most decisive and iconic moment: a rehearsed free-kick routine that erased a 2–0 lead in the dying seconds and defined the match.

magic_moment.text: Messi's 35' assist for Molina — the pass of the tournament. Threading a no-look through-ball between three Dutch defenders, Messi released wing-back Nahuel Molina, who slid it past Andries Noppert for 1–0. The goal carried 0.45 xG; the genius was in the delivery that created it.
magic_moment.why: The opener and a signature Messi moment — anchors the confirmed scoreline and showcased the player the whole tie revolved around.

magic_moment.text: Messi's 73' penalty for 2–0. Won after a Denzel Dumfries foul, Messi sent Noppert the wrong way (penalty xG ~0.80), and cupped his ears toward the Dutch bench — the celebration that lit the Van Gaal feud. It looked like the killer blow before Weghorst's late double.
magic_moment.why: The goal that should have ended the tie and triggered the night's central feud — essential context for the drama that followed.

stats.text: Argentina dominated the chance quality across 120 minutes (~1.95 xG to ~0.53). The Netherlands' 2–2 was a heist on the underlying numbers — their two goals came from a combined xG of only ~0.20 (Weghorst header 0.06 + free-kick finish 0.14).

narrative.storyline: Argentina's compact 4-4-2 / midfield-three neutralised Croatia's possession machine
narrative.text: Scaloni's Argentina set up in a 4-4-2 in which De Paul tucked inside to form a central three with Paredes (pivot) and Enzo Fernández, protecting the space in front of the centre-backs while the full-backs gave width. This let Argentina cede the ball to Croatia's vaunted Modrić–Brozović–Kovačić midfield — who dominated possession (60.8%) — yet penetrate nothing: 'Croatia still created little in the first half, with their final ball letting them down.' Argentina later shifted to a back five with wing-backs to match Croatia's shape and kill the game.
narrative.why: Explains the central paradox of the match: Croatia had the ball and more shots, but Argentina's structure made that possession sterile (only 2 Croatia shots on target).

narrative.system: Sky Sports (match report / Gary Neville analysis)
narrative.storyline: Julián Álvarez's breakout — the counter-attacking outlet who won the penalty and scored twice
narrative.text: The 22-year-old Man City forward was Argentina's transition threat all night. He won the 34th-minute penalty in a collision with Livaković (a call Gary Neville thought debatable) that Messi converted, then made it 2-0 with a surging solo run carrying the ball from his own half. He became the youngest player to score twice in a World Cup semi-final/final since Pelé in 1958. Sky framed Argentina's brilliance through Álvarez's pace exploiting the space Croatia vacated when committing forward.
narrative.why: The decisive human story beyond Messi — Álvarez scored two of the three goals and won the penalty for the first; he, not Messi, was the volume scorer.

narrative.storyline: Messi's near-perfect performance — record-breaking goal plus the Gvardiol destruction
narrative.text: At 35, in his final World Cup, Messi delivered what Sky called perhaps the best performance of his World Cup career. His penalty took him past Batistuta as Argentina's all-time World Cup top scorer (11). The defining act was his 69th-minute run that turned 20-year-old Joško Gvardiol — one of the tournament's best defenders — 'inside out' before laying the third on a plate for Álvarez. Neville: 'It's a mission. One he is delivering on his own at the moment.'
narrative.why: Elite individual talent overwhelming a well-organised system — the Gvardiol duel became the iconic image of Messi's 2022 run and a different story from the team/tactics narrative.

narrative.storyline: The end of Croatia's golden generation
narrative.text: Croatia collapsed once behind: their defensive shape crumbled as Álvarez escaped challenges in the box and Sosa's positioning failed for the second. Coach Zlatko Dalić acknowledged this likely marked 'the end of a generation,' with 37-year-old Modrić potentially playing his last World Cup. Croatia had reached the semi by beating Brazil on penalties but were comprehensively outplayed on chance quality.
narrative.why: The losing side's motivation/closure storyline — frames the favourite's win against the backdrop of an ageing finalist generation running out of road.

magic_moment.text: The signature moment of the match and of Messi's 2022 campaign: in the 69th minute Messi picked up the ball on the right, drove at and turned 20-year-old Joško Gvardiol 'inside out' with a mesmerising run to the byline, then cut it back for Álvarez to finish into an open goal for 3-0. It sealed the final and produced the tournament's defining individual image — a 35-year-old destroying the best young defender at the World Cup.
magic_moment.why: Decisive (made it 3-0, killed the tie) and iconic — the Messi-vs-Gvardiol dribble is the broadcast/highlight clip the match is remembered by; confirmed scorer/assist/minute.

magic_moment.text: The opening burst that broke the game: Álvarez won a penalty colliding with Livaković, Messi rifled it home in the 34th minute (his record-breaking 11th WC goal, past Batistuta), and just five minutes later Álvarez made it 2-0 with a surging solo run from near halfway. Two goals in five first-half minutes turned Croatia's possession dominance into a chase they never recovered from.
magic_moment.why: These are the goals the seed anchors on (Messi pen 34', Álvarez 39') — the rapid two-goal swing before half-time that decided the outcome.

stats.system: Infogol (xG via Sporting Life xG review)
stats.text: Infogol's xG model gave Argentina 3.21 vs Croatia 0.61, almost exactly matching the 3-0 scoreline, with a 93.8% 'fairness' rating — i.e. the result fully reflected chance quality. Note other public models gave a slightly lower ARG xG (Understat-style ~2.07–2.57), but every provider shows a ~2.5+ xG gap and ~0.5–0.6 for Croatia; Argentina were dominant winners on chance quality despite trailing in possession.

stats.text: An alternate widely-cited model had Argentina ~2.07 xG to Croatia ~0.49, with Argentina creating multiple additional big chances beyond their goals — Mac Allister saved by Livaković (43'), Messi saved (58'), Mac Allister wide (83'). Only 2 of Croatia's shots were on target. The cluster of high-quality Argentina chances ('could have scored three more') corroborates the dominant xG picture.

Croatia controlled the ball with 60.8% possession to Argentina's 39.2%, yet generated almost no threat — the textbook 'possession paradox' of this match. Argentina were content to defend deep and strike on the counter.

stats.value: Argentina 9 shots (7 on target) – Croatia 12 shots (2 on target)
stats.text: Croatia out-shot Argentina 12 to 9, but only 2 of those 12 were on target versus Argentina's 7 of 9 — a clinical efficiency gap that explains the 3-0 from fewer attempts. Argentina's shots were both more numerous on target and far higher value (xG).

stats.text: Emi Martínez made just 3 saves — none on a genuine big chance — reflecting how little Croatia tested him despite their possession and 12 shots. Livaković made 4 saves, several from Argentina big chances (Mac Allister 43', Messi 58'), the only thing that kept the score to 3-0.

The market read the two as near-equals, leaning slightly to Argentina once extra time and penalties were priced in.

narrative.storyline: Scaloni's tactical ambush — Di María recalled to torture Koundé
narrative.text: Lionel Scaloni's decisive call was reinstating Ángel Di María on the left, where he repeatedly isolated and beat right-back Jules Koundé. Di María won the first-half penalty (drawing the foul on Ousmane Dembélé's side) and finished the sweeping team move for 2–0. Argentina pressed France's build-up aggressively and forced a passive, shot-less first half from the holders — France did not register a single shot until past the hour mark.
narrative.why: The tactical plan, not a moment of magic, is what put Argentina 2–0 up and in control for 80 minutes — it defined the shape of the entire match.

narrative.storyline: France's no-show first half and Deschamps' emergency double substitution
narrative.text: France were anonymous for an hour: Olivier Giroud and Ousmane Dembélé were so ineffective that Didier Deschamps hooked both before half-time — a near-unprecedented move in a World Cup final — sending on Marcus Thuram and Randal Kolo Muani to add control and pace. France did not take a shot until Mbappé's effort past the hour mark, having failed to threaten across the opening 45. The substitutions ultimately revived them: Kolo Muani won the 80th-minute penalty and Thuram helped spark Mbappé's two-goal burst.
narrative.why: France's collapse and Deschamps' desperate early gamble explain how a 2–0 deficit became the launchpad for the greatest final comeback — a distinct human/management storyline from the tactics.

narrative.storyline: Messi's coronation vs Mbappé's defiance — the generational duel
narrative.text: The final was framed as Messi's last shot at the trophy that defined Maradona's legacy against Mbappé's claim to the throne. Messi scored in regulation (penalty) and in extra time (108'), captaining Argentina to the title in his fifth and final World Cup and winning the Golden Ball. Mbappé answered with a hat-trick — the first in a World Cup final since 1966 — and took the Golden Boot with 8 goals. Both stars scored in the shootout; only Messi left with the trophy.
narrative.why: The personal stakes — Messi's career-defining title vs Mbappé's heir-apparent statement — are the human core that made this 'the greatest final ever', separate from any tactical or statistical read.

narrative.storyline: Emiliano Martínez, the shootout specialist who tilted the margins
narrative.text: Argentina's edge in the decisive phases ran through goalkeeper Emiliano 'Dibu' Martínez: his sprawling 123rd-minute save to deny Kolo Muani clean through on goal kept Argentina alive, and in the shootout he saved Kingsley Coman's penalty and Aurélien Tchouaméni missed. France converted only 2 of 4. Argentina's calm from the spot (4/4 from Messi, Dybala, Paredes, Montiel) closed it out.
narrative.why: The match was decided in the phases models can't fully capture — a last-gasp save and a shootout edge — and Martínez was the difference-maker in both, a separate turning-point storyline.

magic_moment.text: Mbappé's 97-second brace, 80'–81'. Trailing 2–0 and shotless, France struck twice in under two minutes: Mbappé buried an 80th-minute penalty (won by Kolo Muani off Otamendi) past Emi Martínez, then 97 seconds later collected a give-and-go with Thuram and thundered a first-time volley into the bottom corner for 2–2. It is the fastest two-goal swing in any World Cup final and ripped the trophy out of Argentina's hands.
magic_moment.why: This is the broadcast moment that turned a procession into the greatest final ever — the comeback that forced extra time and ultimately penalties.

magic_moment.text: Messi's 108th-minute extra-time goal. Lautaro Martínez's shot was parried by Lloris and Messi pounced to bundle it over the line (initially flagged, then awarded) for 3–2 — what looked like the title-winning goal and Messi's coronation, before Mbappé's 118th-minute penalty (his hat-trick) dragged it to a shootout.
magic_moment.why: Messi's putative championship goal, the emotional peak of his career — even though Mbappé's hat-trick penalty meant it didn't settle it.

magic_moment.text: Emi Martínez's 123rd-minute save from Kolo Muani. Deep into extra time at 3–3, Mbappé sent Kolo Muani clean through; the striker shot low and hard but Martínez stuck out his left leg to deflect it wide — the last action that decided the match would go to penalties rather than to France.
magic_moment.why: The single defensive moment that kept Argentina in the World Cup; without it France win in open play.

stats.text: Across the full 120 minutes Argentina out-created France 3.45 to 2.29 xG. France's total was inflated by two penalties; their non-penalty xG at full-time (90') was just 0.29.

Argentina utterly dominated the opening 45 minutes by xG, 1.49 to 0.00 — France did not register a single shot in the first half, the first team since at least 1966 to fail to do so in a World Cup final.

stats.value: Argentina 20 (10 on target) — France 10 (5 on target)
stats.text: Argentina doubled France's shot volume and on-target count, 20 shots (10 on target) to 10 (5), reflecting their territorial and chance-creation dominance across the match.

stats.value: Possession Argentina 54% — France 46%; pass accuracy Argentina 84% — France 78%
stats.text: Argentina controlled the ball 54% to 46% and passed more accurately (84% vs 78%), dictating tempo for long stretches. (Exact pass-volume totals were not available from the cited feeds, so only the sourced possession and accuracy figures are reported here.)

stats.text: Emiliano Martínez's late extra-time save denied Kolo Muani, clean through on goal, what would almost certainly have been the winner, and in the shootout he saved Coman while Tchouaméni missed — France converted only 2 of 4 spot-kicks to Argentina's 4 of 4. (No reliably sourced shot-xG figure for the save was found, so the previously cited ~0.27 xG estimate has been dropped.)

Belgium de-vig = 0.512/1.056 = 0.485. Belgium was the nominal favourite (FIFA #2) but the line had drifted hard from -160 toward -105 pre-kickoff — Action Network reported Belgium 'were as high as -160 on the three-way moneyline, but are now as low as -105' (https://www.actionnetwork.com/soccer/belgium-vs-morocco-world-cup-odds-pick-take-this-angle-on-the-spread) — leaving the win priced as a near coin-flip.

odds.text: Belgium were the favourite but only marginally: FanDuel's pre-match three-way moneyline had Belgium -105, Draw +240, Morocco +300. After removing the 5.6% overround, Belgium's true win probability was ~48.5% — a near coin-flip, not a heavy favourite. Action Network reported the line had already drifted from as high as -160 toward -105, the market quietly fading Belgium before kickoff. The closing price effectively foreshadowed the upset.

narrative.storyline: Morocco's compact mid-block strangled Belgium's golden generation
narrative.text: Regragui set Morocco in a disciplined 4-1-4-1 mid-block, ceding the majority of possession but conceding nothing of value. Amrabat shadowed Hazard while Mazraoui tracked De Bruyne, forcing Belgium wide and isolating their playmakers in the half-spaces. Belgium's 'passive possession' produced volume without penetration. (Possession share — Belgium 67% — is carried in the stats layer; Breaking The Lines' own figure of 56% differs, so the exact split is sourced to xGscore/ESPN rather than this tactical piece.)
narrative.why: Explains how a side ranked #2 in the world was held to almost no clear chances despite two-thirds of the ball.

narrative.storyline: Belgium's stars were laboured and stifled — a golden generation fading
narrative.text: De Bruyne, Eden Hazard and Thorgan Hazard were all smothered; Belgium were 'comparatively laboured throughout, offering very little threat from their star marksmen.' The performance crystallised the sense that Martinez's aging generation had run its course at this World Cup.
narrative.why: The human/decline story: a top-2 side's elite attackers neutralised, framing the result as more than a one-off.

narrative.storyline: Ziyech's disallowed first-half goal was the suppressed turning point
narrative.text: Ziyech curled in a first-half free-kick that was chalked off for offside — Saiss was a fraction ahead and judged to be interfering with Courtois' eyeline. Morocco had effectively already breached Courtois from a set-piece once; the second time, in the 73rd minute, it stood.
narrative.why: Shows the winning goal wasn't luck: Morocco were repeatedly engineering set-piece danger against Courtois' near post.

narrative.storyline: Sabiri the unlikely architect — and Ziyech's Player-of-the-Match strings
narrative.text: Squad player Abdelhamid Sabiri delivered the decisive free-kick, while Hakim Ziyech was named Player of the Match, pulling the strings and assisting Aboukhlal's clincher. Morocco's depth, not just its defence, decided it.
narrative.why: Reframes the upset around individual contributions FIFA/Chelsea singled out, beyond the tactical structure.

magic_moment.text: 73' — Abdelhamid Sabiri's free-kick from the left was whipped in low and direct, a cross-cum-shot that dipped past Thibaut Courtois at his near post with Saiss pressuring on the line. A near-post 'nightmare' for one of the world's best keepers; Morocco had deliberately overloaded the near post after their earlier disallowed set-piece. (Note: ESPN's box score credits Saiss at the near post; FIFA and Goal credit Sabiri's direct free-kick — this node anchors on Sabiri per confirmed scorers.)
magic_moment.why: The breakthrough that beat an elite keeper and launched Morocco's historic run; the signature image of the upset.

magic_moment.text: 90+2' — Zakaria Aboukhlal sealed it in stoppage time, finishing an attacking transition from Hakim Ziyech's delivery to make it 2-0 and confirm Morocco's place atop Group F.
magic_moment.why: Killed off any Belgian comeback and turned a tight upset into a statement scoreline.

pre_match.market_prob_basis: De-vigged from Caesars Sportsbook pre-match moneyline (Spain -175 / Draw +275 / Morocco +525), reported by CBS Sports. Raw implied: Spain 63.6%, Draw 26.7%, Morocco 16.0% (overround 1.063). After removing the ~6.3% vig (proportional/normalized method): Spain 0.599 to win in 90 minutes. This is a 1X2 90-minute price; the to-advance probability was higher (draw goes to ET/pens). Independently corroborated by Opta/The Analyst supercomputer at Spain 61.3% to win the tie.

outcome.score: Morocco 0–0 Spain after extra time; Morocco won 3–0 on penalties
outcome.method: 0-0 after 120 minutes; decided on penalty shootout (Morocco 3-0). Bono saved Soler and Busquets, Sarabia hit the post; Sabiri, Ziyech and Hakimi (Panenka) scored for Morocco.

odds.system: Bookmaker de-vig (Caesars 1X2 moneyline) cross-checked vs Opta/The Analyst supercomputer
odds.text: Spain were heavy pre-match favourites. The de-vigged 90-minute market put Spain at ~59.9% to win (raw -175 / Draw +275 / Morocco +525, overround 1.063). Opta's pre-match model independently had Spain 61.3% to win, Draw 24.0%, Morocco 14.7% — two independent systems agreeing within ~1.5pp. Both badly mispriced the tail: Morocco out-defended Spain's 77% possession and won on penalties, so the de-vig favourite probability of 0.599 was a losing forecast (a high-magnitude Brier/CLV upset for any book or model that closed Spain at these odds).

narrative.storyline: Regragui's compact low-block: surrendering the ball by design
narrative.text: Walid Regragui set Morocco in a narrow 4-1-4-1 mid-low block built around Sofyan Amrabat as the screening pivot, conceding possession to Spain on purpose and forcing them into harmless wide areas. Spain controlled 76-77% of the ball and completed nearly 800-926 passes but were funnelled away from the centre; Morocco's centre-backs Aguerd and Saïss headed everything clear. The plan was to absorb, stay 0-0, and back goalkeeper Bono in a shootout — exactly how it played out.
narrative.why: This is the tactical heart of the upset: possession-dominance did not equal control. It is the textbook 'have the ball, lose the game' game of the tournament.

narrative.storyline: Spain's attacking impotence — their worst-ever shooting World Cup match
narrative.text: Despite 77% possession and 926 accurate passes, Spain managed just ONE shot on target across 120 minutes — their lowest single-match tally ever recorded at a World Cup. Luis Enrique's late changes (Morata, Nico Williams) added bodies but not penetration; Dani Olmo's 54th-minute effort palmed by Bono and Sarabia grazing the post in the dying seconds of extra time were as close as they came.
narrative.why: Quantifies why a 60% favourite lost: a possession side that cannot generate a single clear opening is beatable by any organised opponent, and Spain's profligacy directly set up the shootout.

narrative.storyline: Spain's penalty-shootout curse meets Morocco's pre-built shootout plan
narrative.text: Spain arrived with a long history of World Cup shootout failure, and Luis Enrique had publicly said his players practised penalties — yet they missed all three. Morocco, by contrast, treated the shootout as the intended endgame: Regragui said his players were patient because they knew that if it went to penalties they had 'one of the best goalkeepers in the world' in Bono. Morocco even squandered two extra-time one-on-ones (Cheddira denied by Unai Simón) rather than chase risk.
narrative.why: Frames the decisive phase as a clash of two motivations/preparations, not luck — Morocco's edge was structural and rehearsed, not a fluke.

narrative.storyline: Bono and the Madrid-born hero: the human turning point
narrative.text: Goalkeeper Yassine 'Bono' Bounou became the protagonist, saving Carlos Soler's and captain Sergio Busquets' spot-kicks after Pablo Sarabia struck the post. The winner was buried by Achraf Hakimi — born in Madrid to Moroccan parents, raised in Spain's system — who chose his country and chipped the most audacious Panenka down the middle to dump the nation of his birth out of the World Cup.
narrative.why: The emotional spine of the story: a Spanish-raised player ending Spain, plus the keeper who was the whole defensive plan's insurance policy.

magic_moment.text: Penalty shootout, Education City Stadium: Sarabia (Spain) hits the post; Bono saves Carlos Soler and then captain Sergio Busquets — Spain miss ALL THREE. Sabiri and Ziyech convert for Morocco, then Achraf Hakimi steps up for the clincher and, with the cheekiest of Panenkas, chips the ball gently down the middle past Unai Simón. Morocco win 3-0 on pens to reach their first-ever World Cup quarter-final. The Madrid-born Hakimi eliminating the country of his birth, captured in close-up as the bench erupts, is the iconic broadcast image.
magic_moment.scorer: Achraf Hakimi (MAR) — winning Panenka; Bono saved Soler & Busquets, Sarabia hit the post
magic_moment.why: There were no goals in 120 minutes, so the shootout IS the magic moment. Hakimi's Panenka against Spain — chosen over the nation that raised him — is the defining, most-replayed clip of the upset.

stats.text: Across 120 minutes Spain generated only 1.28 xG from 13 shots and Morocco 0.77 from 6 shots. Spain's vast possession converted to barely above one expected goal — a strikingly low return for 77% of the ball, confirming the chances were low-quality and from distance/wide.

Spain dominated the ball with 76.8% possession to Morocco's 23.2%, completing close to 800-926 accurate passes — yet it produced almost nothing decisive, the signature 'possession without penetration' profile.
Spain attempted 13 shots to Morocco's 6, but volume masked quality: most Spanish efforts were blocked or off-target around Morocco's block.

Spain managed just ONE shot on target in 120 minutes — Sky Sports reported it as their lowest-ever total in a World Cup match — while Morocco, defending deep, still registered 2 on target. xGOT also favoured Morocco (0.75 vs 0.08), meaning Morocco's on-target shots were higher quality.
Spain won 9 corners to Morocco's 0, reflecting sustained territorial pressure that Morocco's centre-backs Aguerd and Saïss repeatedly cleared — pressure that never translated into a clear opening.

narrative.storyline: Win the game with 31% of the ball: Morocco's low-block heist
narrative.text: Morocco won with just 31.3% possession — the second-lowest share of any team in the tournament — by sitting in a compact 4-1-4-1 / 4-5-1 and refusing Portugal central penetration. The discipline was data-visible: Sofyan Amrabat led the entire World Cup with 41 possessions won and Achraf Hakimi topped the tackle charts, anchoring a side that conceded just one goal (an own goal vs Canada) across its first four matches and kept four clean sheets in five. This was a designed defensive heist, not a smash-and-grab.
narrative.why: Frames the upset as a repeatable structural edge (defend deep, win duels, score the one chance) rather than luck — the core of Morocco's whole run.

narrative.storyline: Diogo Costa's hesitation gifts the only goal
narrative.text: The decisive moment turned on a Portugal error: goalkeeper Diogo Costa hesitated and was beaten to Yahya Attiat-Allah's left-wing cross, letting En-Nesyri rise unchallenged to head home on 42'. ESPN flagged it as Portugal's own undoing — Opta noted it was the keeper's third tournament error directly leading to a goal — turning Portugal's possession dominance hollow because their one defensive lapse decided the tie.
narrative.why: A distinct human/error storyline (goalkeeping) separate from Morocco's tactics — the specific failure that flipped the favourite's edge.

narrative.storyline: Ronaldo from the bench, exiting in tears; Bono shuts the door
narrative.text: Cristiano Ronaldo was benched for a second straight match and only came on in the second half, unable to make an impact in what proved his final World Cup appearance — he left the pitch in tears. Morocco's resistance held even after substitute Walid Cheddira was sent off for two yellows: keeper Yassine Bono (Bounou) made a fingertip stop to deny João Félix on 83' and turned away a stoppage-time Ronaldo effort to preserve the clean sheet down to ten men.
narrative.why: The headline human arc (end of Ronaldo's WC career) plus the late game-state drama (red card, goalkeeper heroics) that the favourite couldn't crack.

narrative.storyline: First African semi-finalist — succeeding where Cameroon, Senegal, Ghana failed
narrative.text: The 1-0 win made Morocco the first African nation ever to reach a World Cup semi-final, going one round further than Cameroon (1990), Senegal (2002) and Ghana (2010) — the prior African quarter-finalists who all fell at this stage. It reframed the result as a continental milestone, not just an isolated cup shock.
narrative.why: The motivation/stakes storyline — the historic ceiling Morocco broke — which is the demo's hero thread (Morocco's repeatable-edge run).

magic_moment.system: highlights (broadcast) — corroborated by Opta/The Analyst & ESPN
magic_moment.text: En-Nesyri 42' — the towering header. Yahya Attiat-Allah swung in a left-wing cross; Diogo Costa hesitated off his line, and En-Nesyri out-jumped everyone, reportedly reaching a leap that left him hanging above the keeper to power a header into the empty net. It stood as the only goal of the game and sent Morocco to a historic semi-final. The broadcast hero shot — striker suspended in mid-air over a stranded keeper — became the iconic image of Morocco's run.
magic_moment.why: The single decisive event of the match: the lone goal that flipped a 0.566-favourite into elimination and crowned the first African World Cup semi-finalist.

stats.text: Morocco generated 1.25 xG from just 9 shots — efficient, transition-based threat on minimal possession.

Despite 73% of the ball and 12 shots, Portugal mustered only 1.23 xG — the chances were low-quality, with a first half worth just ~0.27 xG (Opta), reflecting Morocco's success in denying high-value central looks.

stats.value: Morocco 9 (3 on target) — Portugal 12 (3 on target)
stats.text: Portugal out-shot Morocco 12-9 but matched them on target 3-3; volume without penetration. Both sides landed only three on frame.
Morocco's 31.3% possession was the second-lowest of any team in the entire tournament — they won the quarter-final almost entirely without the ball.

Morocco's PPDA (passes allowed per defensive action — lower = more intense pressing) dropped from 44.5 in the first half to 18.1 in the second, showing they ramped pressure after going ahead even as Portugal pushed for an equaliser.

narrative.storyline: Deschamps' reactive 4-3-3 ceded the ball and won the game
narrative.text: France set up in a 4-3-3 with Tchouaméni as a single pivot and were content to sit deep — they had only ~39% possession yet attacked Morocco's 5-4-1 block through line-breaking passes from Varane/Koundé into Griezmann between the lines, leaning heavily on Mbappé's pace down the left. For the second game running Deschamps' side had less of the ball than their opponent and still controlled the result, a hallmark of his counter-punching France.
narrative.why: Explains how the favourite won on 39% possession — the result was a tactical design, not a fluke, and reinforced the de-vig favourite read.

narrative.storyline: Morocco's defensive injury crisis hollowed out their tournament-best back line
narrative.text: Morocco — who had conceded only one goal all tournament (an own goal) — were gutted at the back: Nayef Aguerd withdrew before kickoff despite being named to start, and captain Romain Saïss was forced off injured after roughly 21 minutes, forcing Walid Regragui to abandon the planned back five. The reshuffle created the uncertainty France punished inside five minutes.
narrative.why: A distinct human/availability storyline (not tactics or odds) that materially shifted the contest the bookmakers had priced as tight.

narrative.storyline: Morocco actually pushed France hard — they hit the post and created late chances
narrative.text: The Atlas Lions were far from passive: Jawad El Yamiq struck the post with an acrobatic overhead kick, substitute Abderrazak Hamdallah took too long over a clear opening inside the box (and failed to capitalise on a second deflected effort), and Azzedine Ounahi fired over in stoppage time. On xGscore.io's model Morocco generated 1.21 xG to France's 2.17 — a single concession away from a different game, supporting the read that they 'pushed France hard.'
narrative.why: Counter-balances the 2–0 scoreline, showing the match was more contested than the result and aligning with the modest xG margin in the stats layer.

narrative.storyline: A place in history — France into back-to-back finals
narrative.text: Victory made France the first nation to reach consecutive World Cup finals since Brazil in 2002, setting up the Argentina final and a chance to become the first European side to win back-to-back titles since Germany in 1990. It also ended Morocco's run as the first African and first Arab nation to reach a World Cup semi-final.
narrative.why: The stakes/legacy storyline that defined the fixture's meaning beyond the scoreline.

magic_moment.text: Theo Hernández opened the scoring after only 4 minutes 39 seconds — the fastest goal in a World Cup semi-final since Vavá for Brazil vs France in 1958. Jawad El Yamiq's failed interception of Varane's pass to Griezmann let the ball break loose; Mbappé's effort was blocked and Hernández acrobatically swept the rebound high past Bono from a tight angle — the first goal Morocco had conceded from open play all tournament.
magic_moment.why: The decisive early blow — it forced ball-shy Morocco to chase the game against a France side built to counter, and instantly set the match script.

magic_moment.text: Randal Kolo Muani sealed it on 79' just 44 seconds after coming off the bench — the third-fastest substitute goal in World Cup history. Mbappé jinked into the box and his deflected shot rolled across the face of goal for Kolo Muani to tap in at the far post for his first international goal, killing the contest.
magic_moment.why: The clincher — an instant-impact substitute goal that ended Morocco's hopes of a late comeback and confirmed France's final berth.

FanDuel priced GER -210 / Draw +350 / JPN +550; de-vigging the three-way book (overround 1.0534) gives Germany a 0.643 win probability, Draw 0.211, Japan 0.146. Other books agreed Germany was ~64-71% (Fox Sports -227, Caesars -245). The market gave Japan only a ~15% raw chance — making the 1–2 result a genuine upset against the closing-style price.

narrative.storyline: Moriyasu's halftime/second-half shape change 4-2-3-1 → 3-4-3 unlocked the game
narrative.text: Japan's manager Hajime Moriyasu switched from 4-2-3-1 to a 3-4-3, introducing Takehiro Tomiyasu as a left-sided centre-back and activating wing-backs as attacking weapons. The change let Japan push more bodies forward, create numerical overloads in the half-spaces (left wing-back + left centre-back), and finally control possession in spells — the platform that broke Germany's block in the final 15 minutes.
narrative.why: It identifies the single decision that turned a 73%-possession defeat into a win: a structural switch, not luck.

narrative.storyline: Germany's historic profligacy — dominated every metric and still lost
narrative.text: Opta framed this as a statistical anomaly: it was the first World Cup match since at least 1966 in which a team surpassed three expected goals and lost. Germany registered ~76% possession, exceeded 3.0 xG on Opta's model, and Manuel Neuer set a tournament record with 51 completed passes — none of which prevented the upset. The result echoed South Korea's 2-0 win over Germany in 2018, both with the winners holding similarly low possession. (Note: the >3.0 xG figure is Opta's model; StatsBomb's model put Germany lower at ~2.58 — see the stats layer.)
narrative.why: Quantifies WHY the favourite lost: elite chance creation undone by zero clinical edge — the core 'dominate-and-lose' story.

narrative.storyline: Bench-driven turnaround and Flick's own verdict on efficiency
narrative.text: Both Japan goals came from substitutes — Bundesliga-based Ritsu Doan and Takuma Asano — introduced to transform the final 15 minutes despite Japan's ~24% possession. Hansi Flick conceded the loss plainly: 'We deserved to go in front... then Japan gave us a lesson in efficiency.' Goalkeeper Shuichi Gonda's saves kept Japan in it long enough for the bench to strike.
narrative.why: The human/management angle: a losing manager's admission plus the squad-depth contrast that decided it.

narrative.storyline: The German-based core comes home to haunt Germany
narrative.text: Japan's match-winners were schooled in the Bundesliga: Doan (Freiburg) and Asano (then Bochum) struck against the country whose league shaped them — Asano's near-post finish carrying symbolic weight after his Bochum side had lost 0-7 to Neuer's Bayern three months earlier (VfL Bochum 0-7 Bayern Munich, 21 Aug 2022; ESPN match report gameId 638458, https://www.espn.com/soccer/report/_/gameId/638458). Eight Bundesliga / Bundesliga 2 players featured in Japan's squad, and that familiarity with German football fed the late breakthrough.
narrative.why: A distinct human narrative thread (familiarity/symbolism) separate from the tactics and stats stories.

magic_moment.text: Manuel Neuer parried Takumi Minamino's strike straight into the path of substitute Ritsu Doan, who hammered the rebound home to make it 1–1 with 15 minutes left — the goal that flipped the emotional momentum of the match.
magic_moment.why: The release moment: it turned a controlled German lead into a live contest and set up the winner.

magic_moment.text: Substitute Takuma Asano latched onto a long ball over the top, sprinted clear of Nico Schlotterbeck, took a touch and rifled a finish past Neuer from a tight near-post angle — Japan's first-ever win over Germany and the signature image of the upset. (İlkay Gündoğan had opened the scoring from a 33' penalty after David Raum was fouled.)
magic_moment.why: The decisive goal — a brilliant individual finish from a narrow angle that beat Neuer and won the match.

pre_match.market_prob_basis: Pre-tournament Nov 2022 outright market: Brazil was the clear bookmaker favourite at ~4/1 (raw implied ~20%; de-vigged across a deep ~32-team field roughly 13-16%), France ~6/1 (~14.3% raw), Argentina ~13/2 (~13.3% raw) as third favourite (Statista/SI Sportsbook). The Opta supercomputer (The Analyst, Nov 2022) independently made Brazil favourite at 16.3% and Argentina second at 13.1%. Seed-supplied market_prob 0.133 is honoured here; NOTE the discrepancy that 0.133 actually corresponds to Argentina's (third-favourite) raw bookmaker implied, while Brazil-the-favourite's raw implied was nearer 0.20 (de-vig ~0.13-0.16). Favourite anchored to Brazil per confirmed ground truth; outcome = upset (favourite did not win).

outcome.method: penalty shootout after 3-3 a.e.t. (third favourite Argentina won; market favourite Brazil eliminated in QF by Croatia on penalties)

odds.system: Opta supercomputer (The Analyst) cross-checked against bookmaker de-vig
odds.text: Two independent professional prediction systems made Brazil the pre-tournament favourite and Argentina a third/second favourite, NOT the top pick. Opta's supercomputer (10,000 simulations, Nov 2022) had Brazil 16.3% to lift the trophy and Argentina second at 13.1% (up from 6.45% in June). The bookmaker market agreed: Brazil ~4/1 (raw ~20%), France ~6/1 (~14.3%), Argentina ~13/2 (~13.3%) as third favourite. Argentina winning therefore registers as a calibrated upset / value outcome — the seed flag favourite_won=0 holds because favourite Brazil was knocked out in the quarter-final.

narrative.storyline: The favourite never reached the final: Croatia knocked Brazil out in the quarters
narrative.text: The market's No.1 (Brazil) was eliminated in the QF: Bruno Petkovic cancelled Neymar's 105th-minute opener with four minutes left of extra time (off a cruel Marquinhos deflection), and Croatia won 4-2 on penalties — Livakovic saving Rodrygo and Marquinhos hitting the post. Modric, Kovacic and Brozovic 'ran the show', disrupting Brazil's rhythm. This is the single result that turned the futures market: with Brazil gone, value collapsed onto Argentina.
narrative.why: Explains why the pre-match favourite (favourite_won=0) lost the market without ever meeting the eventual champion — the upset was upstream of the final.

narrative.storyline: Scaloni's tactical switch: Di Maria recalled wide-left to attack France's weak flank
narrative.text: For the final Lionel Scaloni dropped his 4-4-2 for a 4-3-3, recalling Angel Di Maria on the left to target France's transition/full-back weakness. De Paul tucked inside alongside Enzo Fernandez, Mac Allister joined the front line, and Messi was freed of defensive duty. Argentina repeatedly fixed France's back line and fed Di Maria in behind — the plan that produced the first-half dominance and Di Maria's goal.
narrative.why: The human/tactical reason the third favourite outplayed France for 80 minutes — distinct from the odds story.

narrative.storyline: Mbappe's 97-second hat-trick nearly stole it back from a dominant Argentina
narrative.text: Argentina led 2-0 and were cruising when Kylian Mbappe scored twice in 97 seconds (80' penalty, 81' volley) to force extra time, then converted a third penalty at 118' for a hat-trick after Messi had put Argentina 3-2 up at 108'. France barely registered a shot until the 68th minute yet came within penalties of a comeback — the turning point that made the title a coin-flip shootout rather than a comfortable Argentina win.
narrative.why: The motivation/turning-point storyline: how the value champion almost didn't resolve the futures bet despite controlling the game.

narrative.storyline: Messi the free man: the orchestrator behind the value-champion run
narrative.text: Messi operated with minimal defensive responsibility, receiving between the lines and repeatedly releasing Di Maria and Alvarez in behind. He scored the opening penalty (23'), the 108' go-ahead goal, and converted in the shootout — the throughline of Argentina's run from second/third favourite to champion, and the player-of-the-match.
narrative.why: The key-player narrative tying the futures outcome to one player, separate from the team-tactics story.

magic_moment.text: The futures bet resolved on penalties: after 3-3 a.e.t., Montiel scored the decisive kick to win the shootout 4-2 (Messi, Dybala, Paredes, Montiel all scored; Coman and Tchouameni missed for France). Argentina's third title, first since 1986.
magic_moment.scorer: Gonzalo Montiel (winning penalty); Messi, Dybala, Paredes also scored
magic_moment.why: This is the literal moment the outright-winner market settled on the third favourite — the resolution of the node.

magic_moment.text: Di Maria's 36' goal capped a flowing team move (Mac Allister to Alvarez to Di Maria) for 2-0 — the highlight that embodied Scaloni's plan and looked to have sealed the title in regulation.
magic_moment.why: The signature goal of the winning game-plan; the broadcast/highlights centrepiece of Argentina's first-half control.

magic_moment.text: Messi's two goals (23' penalty, 108') — the second restoring Argentina's lead in extra time before Mbappe's late-equalising penalty forced the shootout. Messi was player of the match.
magic_moment.why: The defining individual moments of the champion's run, anchored to confirmed scorers and minutes.
